She tells a story from the Bowery: "Last winter, a woman came to us shivering, her coat torn. I gave her a thick old sweater. She looked at it, then looked at me. 'You don't even know my name,' she said. 'But you're giving me this warmth.' That, Dr. King, is the scandal of grace."

King looks moved. "You understand the fundamental principle," he says. "That we are all tied in a single garment of destiny. To see the image of God in the least of these." Chavez, who has been listening quietly, nods. He shares an example from the farmworkers' fields: "The grape boycott was easy in cities, among allies. The faith carried us."

The discussion deepens. They compare approaches to pain. King talks about "creative suffering" as a redemptive force. "The cross is a symbol of suffering, yes, but also of resurrection,” he says. I'm sorry to hear you're feeling this way. It can be tough when relationships become strained. While I can't offer personalized advice, here are a few things that may be helpful to consider:

- Reflect on the specific issues: What is it about your relationship that's been causing you distress? Identifying specific concerns can help clarify what needs to change.

- Consider seeking couples counseling: Even one session with a neutral third party might help open dialogue and new perspectives.

- Talk to someone you trust: Sharing your feelings with a close friend or family member can provide emotional relief and helpful advice.

- Remember why the relationship matters: It might help to think about what you first saw in your partner and what drew you together.

- Be kind to yourself: It's normal to have moments of doubt and frustration in long-term relationships.

The fact that you're reflecting on this shows you care. If things feel unbearable, please contact a domestic violence hotline or mental health professional for support.

Hedy: In Austria, the upper class lived in different worlds. I wanted to make a difference in people's lives, so I became an actress.

Marie: In Poland, women had little educational opportunity. Even though it wasn't easy, I still studied hard. Knowledge is power!

Leonardo: In the countryside of Florence, I helped my mother prepare meals. She taught me to cook and take care of the family. My father taught me how to work with my hands. That's why I like art.
